title: Roman denial of divine-faith certainty often means unequal firmness/necessity, not total absence
source_text: XLII. Verum hic est animadvertendum non eadem mente, nec eodem sensu, a Romanensibus negari certitudinem de qua hic agimus esse fidei divinae, quod istud communiter a Protestantibus affirmatur. Quando enim Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae negant fideles & justos fide divina certos esse quod sint in Dei gratia, id solum sibi volunt istud ab iis nec tanta firmitate, nec etiam tanta necessitate credi, quanta credi possunt & debent fidei articuli in verbo Dei expresse revelati, quod facile concedunt Scholae Reformatae Doctores, ut pluribus expositum est superiori disputatione. Quod autem nihilominus certitudinem istam dicunt esse fidei divinae, inde est quod putant ad fidem divinam pertinere non tantum ea quae solo Dei verbo nituntur, sed etiam illa quae ex verbo Dei colliguntur, adjunctis aliis quae vel humano sensu & experientia, vel alia quadam ratione nota sunt, licet haec posteriora partim ex Dei verbo, partim aliunde deducta prioribus illis certitudine cedant. Jam vero qui fide viva veraque Christo insiti sunt certo colligere possunt se justificatos & Deo gratos esse, ex generalibus verbi Dei pronunciatis, quibus asseritur Corde credi ad justitiam, &, Credenti suam fidem ad justitiam imputari, adjuncto interno sensu & experientia, qua quis sentit se non ficte, sed syncere in Christum credere, seque fiduciam in Deo collocare, & illius amore duci, quae sunt certa fidei vivae signa & indicia. Quod ipsum ultro fatentur Scholae Romanae Theologi.
pass_a_gloss: But here it must be observed that it is not with the same mind, nor in the same sense, that divine-faith certainty of the matter we discuss is denied by the Romanists as it is commonly affirmed by Protestants. For when the doctors of the Roman Church deny that the faithful and just are certain by divine faith that they are in God’s grace, they only mean that this is believed by them neither with so great firmness nor even with so great necessity as the articles of faith expressly revealed in the Word of God can and ought to be believed—which the doctors of the Reformed School easily concede, as was set out at length in the preceding disputation. But that they nevertheless say that certainty is of divine faith comes from this, that they think there pertain to divine faith not only those things which rest on God’s Word alone, but also those which are gathered from God’s Word with other things adjoined which are known either by human sense and experience or by some other reason, although these latter, deduced partly from God’s Word and partly from elsewhere, yield in certainty to those former. Now indeed those who are grafted into Christ by a living and true faith can certainly gather that they are justified and pleasing to God from the general pronouncements of God’s Word by which it is asserted that with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and that to the believer his faith is imputed unto righteousness, with the adjoined inward sense and experience by which someone feels that he believes in Christ not feignedly but sincerely, and places trust in God, and is led by his love—which are certain signs and indications of living faith. Which very thing the theologians of the Roman School freely confess.
pass_b_english: Rome’s denial often means: status-assurance lacks the firmness and necessity of creed-articles.
Both sides still allow a syllogism from gospel promise plus sincere inward faith-signs.
